content: 1. Pain is described metaphorically as something that drips, akin to paint, and as a paper airplane that cannot be folded correctly, symbolizing frustration or imperfection. 2. The child enjoys engaging in role-playing and make-believe activities, which are essential for imaginative and social development. 3. Verbal aggression is more commonly used than physical aggression; the child may yell angrily rather than resort to hitting to express frustration or make a point. For example, they might threaten exclusion, such as saying, You can't come to my birthday party. 4. Name-calling and taunting are often employed as methods to exclude other children from social groups. 5. The child begins to form close relationships with peers and may start identifying best friends. Psychological Development: Initiative vs. Guilt 6. During the later preschool years (approximately 3.5 years to the age of formal school entry in the U.S.), the child learns to imagine and expand their skills through active play, including fantasy. 7. They develop the ability to cooperate with others and learn to take on leadership roles as well as follow others. 8. If immobilized by guilt, the child may exhibit fearfulness, cling to the edges of social groups, remain overly dependent on adults, and show limitations in the development of play skills and imagination. Physical Development 9. The child gains approximately 3 kg per year, with an average weight of 17–21 kg. 10. Height increases by about 5 cm per year, with an average height of 105–115 cm. 11. The heart rate ranges from 90 to 110 beats per minute, and the respiratory rate is between 20 and 30 breaths per minute. 12. The head size is nearly equivalent to that of an adult. 13. The child may begin to lose deciduous (baby) teeth. 14. The body proportions become more adult-like. 15. The child requires approximately 7,500 J (1,800 calories) daily. 16. Visual acuity is typically 20/20 when assessed using the Snellen E chart. 17. Visual tracking and binocular vision are well-developed. Motor Development 18. The child can walk backward, toe-to-heel, and navigate stairs unassisted, alternating feet. 19. They may learn to perform somersaults, provided they are taught correctly to avoid injury. 20. They can touch their toes without bending their knees and walk along a balance beam. 21. Skipping using alternating feet is a skill they may acquire. 22. The child can catch a ball thrown from a distance of 1 meter (3 feet). 23. They ride a tricycle or wheeled toy with speed and skillful steering, and some may begin learning to ride bicycles with training wheels. 24. They can jump or hop forward ten times consecutively without falling. 25. The child can balance on either foot with good control for ten seconds. 26. They build three-dimensional structures using small cubes by copying a picture or model. 27. They reproduce various shapes and letters, such as squares, triangles, and letters like A, I, O, U, C, H, L, and T. 28. They demonstrate fair control of writing instruments like pencils or markers and may begin coloring within the lines. 29. They can cut along a line with scissors, though not perfectly. 30. Hand dominance is generally well-established. Cognitive Development 31. The child can form a rectangle by combining two triangular pieces. 32. They build steps using a set of small blocks. 33. They understand the concept of same shape, same size. 34. They sort objects based on two dimensions, such as color and form. 35. They classify objects into groups with a single common feature, such as food items, boats, or animals. 36. They comprehend the concepts of smallest and shortest and can arrange objects in order from shortest to tallest or smallest to largest. 37. They identify objects by their serial position, such as first, second, or last. 38. They can count by rote to 20 and beyond, with many children counting up to 100. 39. They recognize numerals from 1 to 10. 40. They understand the concept of less than, such as identifying which bowl has less water. 41. They grasp terms like dark, light, and early, as in I got up early, before anyone else. It was still dark. 42. They relate clock time to daily activities, such as Time to turn on the TV when the little hand points to 5. 43. Some children can tell time on the hour, such as five o'clock or two o'clock. 44. They understand the purpose of a calendar. 45. They recognize and identify coins and may begin counting and saving money. 46. Many children know the alphabet and can name both uppercase and lowercase letters. 47. They understand the concept of half and can determine how many pieces an object has when it is cut in half. 48. They ask numerous questions, such as Why? What? Where? and When? 49. They are eager to learn new things. Language Development 50. The child has a vocabulary of over 1,500 words. 51. They can narrate a familiar story while looking at pictures in a book. 52. They define simple words by their function, such as A ball is to bounce or A bed is to sleep in. 53. They identify and name four to eight colors. 54. They recognize humor in simple jokes and may create their own jokes and riddles. 55. They produce sentences with five to seven words, though longer sentences are not uncommon. 56. They can state their city or town, birthday, and parents' names. 57. They answer the telephone appropriately, call someone to the phone, or take a brief message. 58. Their speech is almost entirely intelligible. 59. They use would and could correctly. 60. They consistently use the past tense of irregular verbs, such as went, caught, and swam. 61. They appropriately use the past-tense inflection (-ed) for regular verbs, such as jumped, rained, and washed. Social Development 62. The child enjoys and often has one or two close friendships. 63. They play cooperatively, though lapses may occur, and they demonstrate generosity, take turns, and share toys. 64. They participate in group play and shared activities with other children, often suggesting imaginative and elaborate play ideas. 65. They show affection and care for others, particularly those perceived as below them or in pain. 66. They are generally compliant with requests from parents or caregivers. 67. They seek comfort and reassurance from adults but are less openly dependent on it. 68. They exhibit better self-control over emotional swings. 69. They enjoy entertaining others and making them laugh. 70. They boast about their accomplishments. Physical Development (5 Years and Older) 71. Height increases by 5–7 cm per year, reaching 105–120 cm. 72. Weight increases by approximately 2 kg per year, with a range of 17–22 kg. 73. Weight gain reflects significant increases in muscle mass. 74. Heart rate and respiratory rates approach those of adults. 75. The body may appear lanky during periods of rapid growth. 76. Baby teeth begin to be replaced by permanent teeth, starting with the two upper front teeth. 77. Vision is typically 20/20; if below 20/40, a professional evaluation is recommended. 78. It is not uncommon for children to be farsighted. 79. Daily energy requirements range from 6,700 J to 7,100 J (1,600–1,700 calories). Motor Development (5 Years and Older) 80. The child gains greater control over large and fine motor skills, with movements becoming more precise and deliberate, though some clumsiness may persist. 81. They enjoy vigorous physical activities such as running, jumping, climbing, and throwing. 82. They may have difficulty staying still. 83. Their attention span increases, allowing them to work on tasks for longer periods, though consistency may vary. 84. They understand concepts of time, such as today, tomorrow, and yesterday, as well as simple motion concepts like some things move faster than others. 85. They recognize seasons and the major activities associated with them.
